title: A Prophet Confronts a King
overview: The prophet Nathan confronts King David over taking Bathsheba and killing her husband Uriah, and David faces the consequences, including the death of a child, the birth of Solomon, and the end of a war.

parts.label: Nathan's story (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Nathan tells what sounds like a real case for the king to judge: a rich man with huge flocks steals a poor man's only, much loved lamb to feed a guest. David, who had many wives yet took Uriah's only wife, angrily condemns the man, going beyond the law's penalty of paying back four sheep for one.

parts.label: You are the man (vv. 7-12)
parts.note: Nathan turns the story on David, reminding him of everything God had given him, including the former king's household, which in that world passed to the new king as a sign of rule. Because David killed Uriah in secret, violence and public shame will come from inside his own family, which the following chapters go on to describe.

parts.label: Confession and sentence (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: David admits he has wronged the LORD and is told his life will be spared. But Nathan says the child born from this affair will die, a hard statement the text gives without softening.

parts.label: The child dies (vv. 15-23)
parts.note: David fasts and lies on the ground pleading for the sick child, then surprises his servants by washing, worshiping and eating once the child has died, because pleading can no longer change anything. His words "I will go to him" may simply mean he too will one day die, though many readers hear a hope of seeing the child again.

parts.label: Solomon is born (vv. 24-25)
parts.note: Bathsheba gives birth to another son, Solomon, a name linked to the word for peace. Through Nathan he is also named Jedidiah, meaning "loved by the LORD," a sign of favor despite how this marriage began.

parts.label: Rabbah is captured (vv. 26-31)
parts.note: Joab, David's commander, takes the city's water supply and calls David to lead the final attack so the victory will carry the king's name, not Joab's. The last verse is unclear in Hebrew: older translations describe torture, while many modern scholars read forced labor, and either way it records harsh treatment of a defeated people.

disagreement: Christians differ over how to understand the child's death, whether God directly punished David through an innocent child or the text describes the fallout of David's sin in the religious language of its time.
think: Why might it be easier to see a wrong clearly in someone else's story than in our own?
